transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-05-05 15:00 UTC | Duration: 52m
Attendees: Avery Chen (Redwood AE), Samir Patel (Redwood SE), Dr. Laura Kim (Medix Head of AI), Jamal Ortiz (Engineering Manager), Priya Rao (Clinical Ops)

00:00 Speaker 1 (Avery): Hey everyone, thanks for joining — quick intro, I'm Avery on the account, Samir's our solutions engineer. Today we want to scope the POC quality eval plan.
00:12 Speaker 2 (Samir): Hi all. we'll cover what success looks like, what data you'll give, workloads, benchmarks and then the quality tests — golden prompts, regression, hallucination, formatting.
00:25 Speaker 3 (Laura): Great, high level we want a POC that proves clinical safety and consistent formatting for patient summaries. We're OK running hosted for POC but we need to know private/dedicated options later.
00:38 Speaker 1 (Avery): Totally, that's what we usually see. quick question on success criteria — is it pass/fail or a sliding score?
00:45 Speaker 4 (Jamal): Prefer pass/fail against a few must-have checks: zero PHI leakage, <=2% hallucination on critical fields, and 99% format conformance for structured outputs.
00:58 Speaker 2 (Samir): Understood. we'll propose both threshold and continuous metrics. For hallucination detection we use reference-anchored checks and clinician spot-checks.
01:12 Speaker 3 (Priya): What do you mean reference-anchored?
01:15 Speaker 2 (Samir): Sorry, jargon — we compare generated content against available structured inputs and flagged facts; for things outside the input we mark as unsupported instead of guessing. That reduces hallucination.
01:30 Speaker 1 (Avery): Okay let's talk dataset size and workload. Jamal, what throughput and record counts are you planning?
01:38 Speaker 4 (Jamal): For the POC we can provide 10k de-identified patient notes plus a smaller 500-case golden set for manual review. Throughput target is 100 concurrent inference qps peak, 20 qps baseline.
01:53 Speaker 2 (Samir): 100 qps peak helps us size batching and model variant. For hosted POC we'll run a benchmark with both quantized 8-bit and FP16 variants — that gives a latency/cost tradeoff.
02:08 Speaker 3 (Laura): Are there known latency SLAs we can expect? We need <=500ms p99 for single-turn summaries.
02:15 Speaker 2 (Samir): 500ms p99 is tight but possible with smaller context and optimized kernels; otherwise we can do 95th percentile to be more realistic. We should record p50/p95/p99 in the spreadsheet.
02:30 Speaker 1 (Avery): Let's define the quality eval plan specifics. We'll deliver an eval spreadsheet with columns: prompt_id, input_snippet, expected_output_format, golden_reference, automated_score, manual_score, pass_fail.
02:45 Speaker 3 (Laura): That sounds good. for golden prompts — we want about 500 diverse prompts covering edge cases: meds, diagnoses, comorbidities, ambiguous notes.
02:55 Speaker 2 (Samir): We'll curate 500 golden prompts from your 10k sample plus 50 clinician-authored edge cases you give. We'll include explicit instructions in prompts to force structured JSON output when needed.
03:10 Speaker 4 (Jamal): How will regression tests run? We want to catch regressions between model versions, quantization, or config changes.
03:18 Speaker 2 (Samir): Regression tests will run on the golden set each time we flip a model or runtime. We'll store previous outputs to diff against new outputs and flag changes exceeding a token-level similarity threshold or structural differences.
03:33 Speaker 1 (Avery): Add to that: false positives where format changes but clinical meaning preserved should be triaged manually — we'll have a human review bucket.
03:45 Speaker 3 (Priya): Hallucination checks — you mentioned automated detection and clinician spot-checks. Can you share the rubric?
03:53 Speaker 2 (Samir): Sure. Automated checks include: entity overlap with input (e.g., medication names, labs), contradiction detection using simple entailment heuristics, and domain-specific validators (like med name lists). We then sample 10% for clinician review focusing on high-risk outputs.
04:12 Speaker 4 (Jamal): For scoring approach, we prefer a combined metric: 60% automated score (format + overlap + classifier), 40% manual clinical score. Automated must catch obvious failures quickly.
04:25 Speaker 1 (Avery): We'll propose a composite score 0-100 with thresholds: >=85 pass, 70-85 review, <70 fail. But we'll let you tweak weightings — Dr. Kim will own final thresholds.
04:40 Speaker 3 (Laura): Sounds reasonable. Also need to ensure logs and audit trace for each inference (input hash, model version, timestamp) for compliance.
04:50 Speaker 2 (Samir): We collect request-level metadata in the POC: model variant, kernel, runtime, token counts, latency, and the full output. We can redact any PII in logs by default; since you'll provide de-identified data it should be straightforward.
05:05 Speaker 4 (Jamal): Security files: send SOC2, ISO docs. We need encryption at rest and KMS integration if it goes private.
05:13 Speaker 1 (Avery): We'll attach the security/compliance pack. For private/dedicated options, that's future phase but we can size it during POC if you want guaranteed throughput.
05:25 Speaker 3 (Priya): Timeline — how long to run benchmarks and get results?
05:30 Speaker 2 (Samir): Typical timeline: week 0 intake + data prep, week 1 run benchmarks and iterate on prompts, week 2 manual review + regression run, week 3 final report and go/no-go. So about 3 weeks total.
05:45 Speaker 4 (Jamal): We have internal stakeholders that need results by end of May. With a May 5 start that fits if deliverables are timely.
05:53 Speaker 1 (Avery): Great. We'll plan for the 3-week window. Now some nitty-gritty on the eval metrics: format conformance will be strict — we use a JSON schema for structured outputs and count schema violations. Schema violations count as automatic fail for that prompt.
06:10 Speaker 2 (Samir): For hallucination percent we compute per-prompt: number of hallucinated facts / total factual claims, expressed as percentage. We'll average across the golden set and report p95.
06:25 Speaker 3 (Laura): Can you detect subtle hallucinations, like inventing a medication dosage?
06:30 Speaker 2 (Samir): We'll flag numeric discrepancies with a numeric validator and cross-check against input where available. But subtle clinical hallucinations often require human review — hence the 40% manual score.
06:45 Speaker 1 (Avery): Discussion shift: benchmarks — we'll run latency and cost profiling across 3 model configs: baseline open model (e.g., Llama variant), quantized low-cost, and a higher-quality FP16 variant. We'll record tokens/sec and cost per 1k tokens approximation.
07:05 Speaker 4 (Jamal): We also want throughput tests with KV cache warm and cold starts since many requests reuse context.
07:12 Speaker 2 (Samir): Yes we'll run both warm and cold KV cache runs and include continuous batching behavior; we'll log throughput, effective latency, and token cost.
07:22 Speaker 3 (Priya): Is it possible to automate format checks? We have many output fields that must be present.
07:27 Speaker 2 (Samir): Absolutely — we validate against your JSON schema and return per-field pass/fail with normalized error messages.
07:36 Speaker 1 (Avery): On golden prompts, please include clinician labels for expected severity and any red flags. That helps us prioritize manual review sampling.
07:46 Speaker 3 (Laura): We'll annotate the 500 golden prompts accordingly.
07:50 Speaker 4 (Jamal): About regression detection — how sensitive are the diffs? We don't want noise due to tokenization differences.
07:56 Speaker 2 (Samir): We'll use a normalized canonicalization: remove whitespace, normalize numbers to a canonical numeric format, and compare structural equality for JSON responses. We'll also compute fuzzy similarity (BLEU-ish or ROUGE-ish) as a backup.
08:15 Speaker 3 (Priya): Any examples of hallucination tests you run?
08:20 Speaker 2 (Samir): One test is knowledge-unsupported claims: we ask the model to assert a fact not provided in input; expected output is "I don't know" or "unsupported". If the model fabricates, that's a fail.
08:33 Speaker 1 (Avery): Also include poisoning/edge-case prompts where inputs are messy — we want robust parsing.
08:38 Speaker 3 (Laura): Good point. we have many legacy notes with shorthand and OCR artifacts.
08:44 Speaker 2 (Samir): We'll add a sub-sample of noisy inputs to the golden set to measure robustness.
08:50 Speaker 4 (Jamal): For scoring, can you output both detailed per-prompt diagnostics and an executive summary?
08:56 Speaker 1 (Avery): Yes; the deliverable will include per-prompt rows in the spreadsheet with automated flags, manual notes, and a final aggregated dashboard with pass rates and cost/latency tradeoffs.
09:10 Speaker 3 (Laura): What about edge-case remediation? If model fails on certain classes, can we push prompt-engineering or fallback policies?
09:18 Speaker 2 (Samir): Yes we'll prototype prompt adjustments, and if needed we can enable deterministic fallbacks like returning structured "review required" or calling a smaller retrieval/QA step.
09:30 Speaker 4 (Jamal): Any vendor lock or model hosting constraints? We care about portability.
09:36 Speaker 1 (Avery): Redwood supports multiple backends; POC will use our hosted runtime but artifacts (prompts, eval scripts) are portable. If you move to Dedicated/Private there are infra options with same API.
09:52 Speaker 3 (Priya): Compliance: will logs contain PII? We asked to keep logs de-identified.
09:57 Speaker 2 (Samir): We'll only log de-identified inputs you provide and can support additional redaction or not log raw text on request.
10:07 Speaker 4 (Jamal): Pricing for the POC? We want an estimate for the 3-week run.
10:13 Speaker 1 (Avery): For a standard hosted evaluation we usually credit a portion for initial benchmarking — we'll send a pricing note, but expect a modest spend to cover dedicated benchmark instances if you want exact p99 numbers.
10:26 Speaker 3 (Laura): Competitors — just so you're aware, we're also evaluating Anthropic and an OpenAI pipeline internally. This is primarily to validate latency and hallucination behavior.
10:38 Speaker 1 (Avery): Understood, we'll make sure to highlight differences in the final report and provide tradeoffs.
10:45 Speaker 2 (Samir): Quick operational note: for the automated scoring we'll include these metrics: format_pass_rate, hallucination_rate (p95), avg_manual_score, p99_latency, tokens_per_dollar.
10:58 Speaker 3 (Priya): For format_pass_rate, is schema violation counted as full fail or partial?
11:03 Speaker 2 (Samir): Schema violation is full fail for that prompt; we'll also count field-level failures for more nuance.
11:12 Speaker 1 (Avery): Let's capture the concrete next steps — we'll confirm owners and due dates.
11:18 Speaker 4 (Jamal): Jamal will hand off the de-identified 10k dataset and 500 annotated golden prompts by May 10.
11:24 Speaker 1 (Avery): Avery will send the eval spreadsheet, golden prompt template, and security pack by May 7.
11:30 Speaker 2 (Samir): I'll prepare the benchmark script and sample runtime configs — due May 12.
11:36 Speaker 3 (Laura): we'll review thresholds internally and respond by May 8.
11:42 Speaker 1 (Avery): Any final Qs?
11:45 Speaker 3 (Priya): Just one — do you support per-prompt manual override flags in the dashboard?
11:50 Speaker 2 (Samir): Yes, the dashboard allows manual override and notes; overrides are versioned.
11:58 Speaker 1 (Avery): Ok thanks everyone. We'll follow up with the artifacts and schedule the first benchmark next week.
12:06 Speaker 4 (Jamal): Thanks.
12:08 Speaker 3 (Laura): Thanks all.
